impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement possesses sufficient exclusionary rights to establish constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue for infringement possess a non-illusory exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license for commercialization. This clarifies the minimum retained rights needed for patentees to maintain standing after licensing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents by preserving the right to sue for infringement, enabling more flexible licensing arrangements without forfeiting enforcement power.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face the prospect of suits by licensors who retain enforcement rights even when they have transferred most commercial exploitation rights, potentially increasing litigation exposure.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's anti-CGRP antibody patents were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112, after the jury found infringement and no invalidity.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache treatment patents covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, finding that the specification's disclosure of one humanized antibody plus known methods of making others was sufficient. This is a major ruling in the ongoing pharmaceutical patent battles over CGRP-pathway migraine treatments worth billions of dollars.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies benefit from a more permissive standard for written description and enablement of genus claims, particularly where the specification discloses representative species plus known methods for generating additional embodiments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face stronger patent barriers, as broader genus claims covering classes of biologics may be more difficult to invalidate under § 112.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing emulated function calls to a model are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether damages for patent infringement can include foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million patent infringement judgment against Norton (Gen Digital), holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and require further proceedings on step two. The court also ruled that the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales, limiting patent damages to domestic activity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from the court's reinforcement that damages for patent infringement cannot be based on extraterritorial sales, limiting patentees' ability to inflate damages with foreign revenue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders, particularly universities and research institutions, face heightened § 101 eligibility challenges for software-related patents and cannot recover damages tied to the infringer's foreign sales.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict was supported by legally sufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether inventorship was properly determined.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret verdict, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets in the cosmetic penile implant industry were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the inventorship correction, vacated the permanent injunction, and vacated the reasonable royalty and exemplary damages awards, while affirming trademark counterfeiting liability.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses benefit from the court's rigorous application of trade secret protectability requirements, limiting plaintiffs' ability to claim trade secret status for information that is generally known in the industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets derive independent economic value from not being generally known, or risk losing enforcement actions.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet filed suit, given that Insulet was aware of misappropriation more than three years prior to filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation of insulin patch pump technology, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred because the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The court found Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the three-year DTSA statute of limitations, providing a clear defense when plaintiffs delay filing suit despite knowledge of misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation; delay beyond three years from discovery will bar federal DTSA claims regardless of the merits.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, finding the claims merely recited conventional data-gathering and processing steps. The court vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney fees under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies in agriculture and IoT benefit from the remand on exceptional case status, as courts may more readily award fees when patentees pursue claims on patents that are clearly ineligible.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech companies and other IoT-focused businesses face continued challenges in patenting data collection and processing systems, as such claims are susceptible to invalidation as abstract ideas under § 101.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate deposition witness may testify on matters outside their personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA § 102(b) requires that a prior-art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate witness may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a device's internal functionality at the time of sale. The court rejected the argument that source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from the ability to use 30(b)(6) witnesses without personal knowledge of historical events at summary judgment, and from the ruling that prior art sales need not explicitly disclose internal functionality to trigger the on-sale bar.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader invalidity challenges under the on-sale bar, as commercial sales of devices more than one year before the priority date may invalidate patents even without evidence that the sale publicly revealed the claimed functionality.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims covering selection of a fastest core in a multicore processor for tasks that cannot run across multiple cores are infringed by chips designed and tested domestically but manufactured abroad, and whether doctrine of equivalents infringement was properly denied.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement on extraterritoriality grounds for VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine disputes of material fact about whether Intel's domestic activities constituted infringement. The court affirmed summary judgment denying VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the ruling that domestic design, testing, and use of patented technology may constitute infringement even when manufacturing occurs abroad, expanding the reach of U.S. patent enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor and technology companies that design domestically but manufacture abroad face increased patent infringement exposure for their domestic design and testing activities.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the jury's infringement and damages findings were supported by sufficient evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility, finding that some claims directed to non-uniform constellation designs may be abstract under Alice, while affirming eligibility for claims with more specific technical implementations. The court also affirmed the infringement and damages findings, including willfulness. The case involves standards-essential technology used in television broadcasting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for more concretely claimed inventions and the substantial damages award.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communications standards face continued patent infringement risk and large damages awards, and broader patent claims in this space may still face § 101 challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents and whether the ITC properly determined Masimo's domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches with blood oxygen features that infringed Masimo's patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models. The court found no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and smaller innovators benefit from the affirmance of ITC enforcement power against major technology companies, demonstrating the ITC as an effective venue for blocking infringing imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant business disruption from ITC exclusion orders, potentially requiring product redesigns or removal of patented features from imported products.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline for seeking a stay of its original declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action, preventing manipulation of the statutory timing requirements. This ruling ensures that parties cannot strategically refile actions to gain mandatory stays they initially forfeited.
impacts.positiveImplications: ITC complainants benefit from the ruling that respondents cannot game the mandatory stay provisions by refiling district court actions, preserving the integrity of ITC investigation timelines.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical and other companies facing ITC investigations lose a potential litigation strategy for pausing parallel district court proceedings, and must carefully comply with statutory stay deadlines in their initial filings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including the fairness of the settlement, the attorneys' fee award, and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that PACER fees exceeded statutory authority, with hundreds of thousands of users receiving full or substantial reimbursement. The court upheld the attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to the nonprofit class representatives, rejecting all objections.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides direct financial recovery to businesses and law firms that regularly use PACER, and the ruling validates incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, supporting future public interest class litigation.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to district court patent litigation may file IPR petitions on the filing deadline of the actual defendant, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding insufficient support for the Board's analysis of dependent claims involving time-delayed reporting of sensor information. The court also addressed but declined to review challenges to Qualcomm's standing as a non-party IPR petitioner filing on the deadline of the actual litigant.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the court's scrutiny of third-party IPR petitions filed on another party's deadline, and from the vacatur requiring the Board to more rigorously analyze obviousness of dependent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on third parties to file IPR petitions as proxies face uncertainty about the procedural legitimacy of such filings, and IPR petitioners must ensure thorough obviousness analysis for each challenged claim.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a single jury verdict question covering infringement of multiple patents, without requiring identification of which patent was infringed, requires a new trial, and whether the district court properly analyzed patent eligibility under Alice step two for building automation system patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment involving smart thermostat technology, holding that the jury's use of a single verdict question covering all asserted patents without identifying which were infringed was prejudicial error requiring a new trial. The court also remanded for further § 101 analysis under Alice step two.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must distinguish between individual patents, preventing general infringement findings that obscure which patents drive liability and damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases must structure verdict forms to require patent-by-patent findings, adding complexity to trial proceedings and potentially weakening their overall damages case.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be measured at a standard temperature of 25°C, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed non-infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's generic drug, holding that the pH limitation must be measured at the standard 25°C temperature consistent with the field and that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents. This clears the path for Mylan's generic competitor to Actelion's hypertension drug Veletri.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from the court's application of standard measurement conditions in claim construction, enabling market entry for generic versions of branded drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection when claim terms reference measurable parameters, as courts will apply standard field conditions rather than allowing patentees to argue for measurements under non-standard conditions.
